claims.text: Classical molecular dynamics simulations can be used to study the size-dependent thermal stability of FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
An appropriate alloy potential, such as an EAM-based potential, can represent FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles in these simulations.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have reduced thermal stability.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have lower melting temperatures.
The proposed initial system consists of as-synthesized FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles ranging from a few to tens of nanometers in diameter.
The nanoparticles initially possess crystalline order at room temperature.
Temperature-ramp MD simulations can reveal the onset of atomic rearrangement and melting for each nanoparticle size.
The simulations can be conducted under controlled thermodynamic conditions using an NPT ensemble.
The simulations require a validated interatomic potential for the quinary alloy.
The simulated temperature range should extend from ambient temperature to above the expected nanoparticle melting point.
Atomic-scale diffusion occurs at both the surface and core during heating.
Surface and core diffusion lead to surface reconstruction and melting behavior.
Smaller nanoparticles have a higher surface-to-volume ratio.
A higher surface-to-volume ratio lowers the energy barrier for melting.
The lower melting barrier in smaller nanoparticles causes disorder to begin at a lower temperature.
Melting temperature and thermal stability will decrease systematically as nanoparticle size decreases.
Bulk FeCuCrCoNi HEAs and larger nanoparticles generally have higher melting points than smaller nanoparticles.
Classical MD may not fully capture quantum effects in very small nanoparticles.
The predicted behavior is sensitive to empirical-potential accuracy and finite-size effects.
Absence of a systematic size dependence under identical simulation conditions would falsify the proposed size-dependent trend.
